newsitem.title: UK: Paper says Major to privatise social services.
newsitem.headline: Paper says Major to privatise social services.

text.p: A British newspaper reported on Sunday that Prime Minister John Major's government is planning the radical step of privatising social services if it wins a general election expected in May.
The Sunday Times said the Conservative administration wants to show voters that it has lost none of its reforming zeal after nearly 18 years in power.

Under the controversial plan, the private sector and voluntary groups would have the right to bid to provide services such as care for the elderly and children that are now largely the preserve of local authorities.
Ministers confirmed that a document would be published next month setting out ways of shaking up the social services.
But junior health minister Gerald Malone declined to comment on the assertion that local authorities would be required to put care contracts out to tender.
He told BBC radio, however, that cooperation between local authorities, voluntary organisations and the private sector was already working well in some parts of Britain.
"One would hope that mechanisms could be looked at which would ensure that that quality of provision and value for money that underpins it could be available more widely," Malone said.

The Sunday Times said privatisation would be a core theme of Major's election manifesto. In addition, the Conservatives would sell off the London underground rail network, if they won a fifth term in office, the paper said.
The main opposition Labour party, which is favoured to win an election now no more than four months away, sees merit in exploring ways of providing social services more efficiently.
Britain spends eight billion pounds ($13 billion) a year on social services and the cost is rising fast.
But Labour health spokesman Chris Smith attacked the reported privatisation plan.
"It seems as if the government is simply getting fixated with the ideological process of privatisation instead of looking at what's actually needed on the ground," he told BBC radio.
